title: SAJ expands product range through growing Lakarcade network | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 17 September 2026 00:00
-     - 9

SAJ Associates Ltd., is expanding its product range through the growing network of Lakarcade, which currently holds a significant share of Sri Lanka’s souvenir and gift market.

Lakarcade has recently strengthened its market presence with the opening of a new souvenir shop at a hotel in Colombo. 

Through its expanding network of showrooms across the country, the company is taking the skills and capabilities of Sri Lankan craftsmen directly to tourists.

SAJ Associates Founder Jayampathy Arambepola said the company was pleased to introduce a new range of products to cater to the increasing number of tourists arriving in Sri Lanka this season.

“We are extremely happy to state that we are moving forward to cater to the increasing tourist arrivals this season with an additional new range of products through the expanding network of Lakarcade.”

He further explained that SAJ Associates had been working closely with Lakarcade for the past one and a half years.

“We initially started with 12 glycerine-based soaps and then expanded our range with another 12 products, comprising four shampoos, four conditioners and four liquid soaps. We are now privileged to add four more face creams and two face washes, bringing our total range to 30 high-quality products targeted at the tourist and diaspora markets.”

Arambepola said Lakarcade’s expanding network of exclusive outlets in key tourist locations would further improve the availability of SAJ products to visitors.

“The expanding network of Lakarcade, with exclusive shops at very important locations, will enhance the availability of our products to tourists,” he said.

He added that Lakarcade’s focus on the specialised tourist gift market, together with its new showrooms, including the outlet at Shangri-La Hotel, would create further opportunities for growth.

“They are in the specialised tourist gift market and have added more showrooms, including one at Shangri-La Hotel. I am sure they will expand further in this segment in the future. They are also satisfying the needs of the Sri Lankan diaspora, which is another growing market. They are looking for quality products to take back to their respective homes as gifts for themselves and others.”

Arambepola said the rapidly expanding tourist industry required specialised, high-quality products capable of meeting international standards.

“They need specialised products like those we produce at SAJ to cater to the fast-expanding tourist market. We are very happy to work with a good company such as Lakarcade. We process high-quality glycerine-based products targeted at international markets, and together we are working to take Sri Lankan product quality to the next level.”

Arambepola also highlighted the positive impact of the expanding distribution network on rural communities involved in the production of specialised ingredients used in SAJ products.

“The huge contribution made through this network will also help more than 500 female farmers who are growing these specialised ingredients in the North Central Province. This will help them achieve better economic conditions, increase their incomes and improve their quality of life. We are very grateful to Lakarcade for supporting these rural women and contributing to their livelihoods,” added.

title: Japanese investor Yoshimichi Watanabe backs Hunas Holdings ahead of expansion | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 17 September 2026 00:00
-     - 19

Japanese investor Yoshimichi Watanabe has entered into a partnership with Colombo Stock Exchange-listed Hunas Holdings PLC, in a move that comes as the diversified conglomerate prepares a significant expansion of its hospitality and real estate interests in Sri Lanka.

The partnership brings foreign capital and international market experience into one of Sri Lanka’s fastest-diversifying listed groups at a point when the Group is actively building out its pipeline across both sectors. Hunas Holdings is currently evaluating a series of hospitality and real estate developments in Sri Lanka, with further announcements expected in the coming months.

Hunas Holdings PLC operates across hospitality and leisure, real estate, renewable energy and agriculture, with a hotel portfolio that includes Hunas Falls in Elkaduwa

For Sri Lanka, the significance of the partnership extends beyond the two parties. Inbound investment of this nature, from an investor with direct and sustained experience of the market, is a measure of returning confidence in the country as a destination and in the underlying fundamentals of its hospitality sector, at a time when the industry is repositioning towards higher-value, experience-led travel.

Watanabe brings investment experience across e-commerce, hospitality and real estate in Japan and in international markets including Bali, Indonesia. He has also maintained a relationship with Sri Lanka over many years, having made multiple investments in the country, giving him first-hand insight into its business environment, regulatory landscape and long-term potential.

While acknowledging the economic pressures Sri Lanka has faced, Watanabe takes a deliberately counter-cyclical view, arguing that the current climate offers a window in which long-term value can be created rather than a reason for caution.

“Having spent many years connected to Sri Lanka, I have seen both its challenges and its remarkable potential,” said Yoshimichi Watanabe. “I understand the economic realities the country has faced, but I also believe this is the moment to look beyond the immediate picture and invest with a long-term perspective. Hospitality and real estate are where I see the clearest opportunity, and in Hunas Holdings I have found a partner with the local strength, the asset base and the ambition to build something meaningful.”

The partnership combines Watanabe’s international investment experience and long-term conviction in Sri Lanka with Hunas Holdings’ established local presence, operating assets and market knowledge, positioning both parties to move quickly as the Group’s expansion plans take shape.

title: Sri Lanka’s creative and lifestyle sector targets Maldivian hospitality market | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 17 September 2026 00:00
-     - 15

In a strategic move to expand Sri Lanka’s export footprint, the Sri Lanka Export Development Board (EDB), in collaboration with the Sri Lanka High Commission in the Maldives and key private sector partners, organised a dedicated Sri Lanka Country Pavilion at the Food and Hospitality Asia Maldives (FHAM) 2026 held from 7 to 9 September, in Hulhumalé, Maldives for Giftware and Lifestyle products sector.

The Sri Lanka country pavilion featured the exclusive/ niche products of the 10 selected SMEs under the “Creative Sri Lanka 2030” national initiative.

The Maldives represents a high-value, tourism-driven market with consistent demand for premium giftware, eco-friendly lifestyle items, home décor, and spa products particularly among luxury resort chains, boutique hotels, and souvenir retailers.

In addition, close geographical proximity offers Sri Lankan exporters, manufacturers lower freight costs, quicker market entry, and easier trade logistics compared to distant international markets.

Sri Lanka’s distinctive craftsmanship, creative talent, cultural diversity, and diverse range of natural raw materials provide a strong foundation for developing innovative, high-value, and internationally competitive products in the giftware and lifestyle sector.

Furthermore, given Sri Lanka’s relatively low-volume production capacity, the sector is well positioned to cater to niche and high-value export markets, where success is driven not by mass production but by superior quality, distinctive design, innovation, and effective marketing strategies that enable Sri Lankan products to differentiate themselves from those of competing countries.

These inherent strengths of Sri Lanka’s giftware and lifestyle industry align well with the growing demand in the Maldivian market and present significant opportunities to integrate Sri Lankan products into the Maldivian hospitality supply chain. In particular, there is strong potential for Sri Lankan products in areas such as home and interior décor, household furnishings, recycled and handmade paper products, wellness and spa items, fashion accessories, and distinctive artisanal souvenirs, thereby creating opportunities for Sri Lankan manufacturers and exporters to establish sustainable market linkages with the Maldivian hospitality sector.

The participant companies represent the “Creative Sri Lanka 2030” program, which aims to globally promote Sri Lankan creative industries centered on ethical, sustainable, and high-value niche production.

FHAM is the Maldives’ leading international exhibition for the food, beverage, and hospitality industries. Held annually, it brings together local and global suppliers, service providers, and professionals to showcase products, build partnerships, and support the country’s tourism-driven economy. 

The exhibition attracts a diverse group of trade visitors, including resort owners and developers, hotel management executives, project consultants and developers, housekeeping managers, dealers, importers, and suppliers, providing exhibitors with valuable opportunities to engage directly with key decision-makers within the hospitality sector.

The participating companies represent the Creative Sri Lanka 2030 Program, which seeks to promote Sri Lanka’s creative industries in international markets, with a strong focus on ethical and sustainable practices, innovation, and the development of high-value niche products.

Furthermore, the participating companies were facilitated to engage with key stakeholders in the Giftware and Lifestyle sector through business networking meetings organised by the Sri Lanka High Commission in Malé with representatives of the Maldives Business Chamber and Maldives Association of Life skills Education (MALE). These interactions provided a valuable platform for knowledge exchange, sharing of market intelligence, exploring potential partnerships, and identifying new business and market opportunities.

This was a valuable opportunity to the Sri Lankan companies to gain direct access to key procurement decision-makers in the Maldivian hotel sector. Participation in FHAM 2026 provided a direct channel to gather market intelligence, observe emerging sustainable trends, and secure long-term trade partnerships, further strengthening regional economic integration and driving Sri Lanka’s rural-based creative economy.

title: Legislating for change: Looking at how quota laws for women in the Boardroom panned out globally | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 17 September 2026 00:00
-     - 12

Sri Lanka’s consistently low rankings on economic gender parity reflect a structural problem that will not resolve itself incrementally. With 40% of the top 30 CSE-listed companies not having a single woman on their Boards, something must change

Sri Lanka’s position on gender parity in economic participation is, frankly, uncomfortable reading. We rank 130th out of 143 countries on the World Economic Forum’s Global Gender Gap Index 2025, and we are the only country in the world to have recorded a negative rate of advancement since 2006. With 99.8% of females receiving the same level of education as males (ranked 48th in the world) and a Health & Survival score of 97.9% (ranked 32nd), we are well-educated, and we are healthy. We simply are not represented in the workforce.

One of the most frequently debated interventions to accelerate female participation in corporate leadership is the introduction of gender quotas. These legislated minimums compel companies to appoint women to their boards, but the debate is often heated: proponents argue that voluntary progress is too slow and too fragile, while critics contend that mandated appointments undermine meritocracy. Setting aside such ideological arguments, let’s take a look at empirical evidence to determine what actually happens when countries pass these laws. This article examines the cases of  Norway, France, and India and asks an honest question: Did the legislation work?

Case Study 1: Norway, the pioneer

Legislation

Norway was the first country in the world to introduce a mandatory gender quota for corporate boards. In December 2003, an amendment to the Norwegian Companies Act was passed requiring a minimum of 40% representation of each gender on the boards of all publicly listed limited liability companies (PLCs). The legislation initially allowed for voluntary compliance, with a deadline of July 2005. When women held only around 12% of board seats by this deadline, the government made the consequences for non-compliance severe. Announced in 2006, companies that failed to meet the quota by January 2008 could be denied registration, dissolved, or subjected to ongoing financial penalties.

Outcomes

The results in terms of board representation were swift and unambiguous. At the time the law was passed, women held approximately 9% of board seats in Norwegian PLCs. By 2008, that figure had reached 43%. The quota was met, and to date it has held.

But the story beyond the boardroom is more nuanced. A 2019 study by economist Marianne Bertrand, published by the National Bureau of Economic Research, found that the quota had no discernible effect on broader female labour market outcomes, wages, or the pipeline of women into senior executive roles. Only 8% of board chairs are women, and women account for just 4% of chief executives and 12% of chief financial officers among Oslo Stock Exchange-listed companies. The quota elevated a few select women into boardrooms, but it did not automatically elevate women throughout organisations.

Another unintended consequence was that a significant number of companies chose to delist rather than comply. Of the 563 firms that were PLCs in 2003, only 179 remained so by 2008. Some converted to private limited company status specifically to avoid the quota requirement.

On financial performance, older studies documented a short-term decline in Tobin’s Q, a measure of firm value, following the law’s announcement and attributed this to boards becoming younger and hence less experienced in the immediate post-quota years. More recent analyses reject any lasting negative impact on firm profitability. What is broadly agreed upon is that the new women directors appointed under the quota were, on average, more highly qualified, better educated, and higher-earning than their female predecessors, disproving the common assumption that quotas compromise quality.

The verdict: Norway’s quota succeeded in its primary goal of achieving gender balance at the board level. Its limitations lie in the absence of spillover effects into the broader organisation and the loophole created by permitting companies to restructure to avoid compliance.

Case Study 2: France, the convert

Legislation

France was not always a champion of legislative intervention, instead choosing to pursue a ‘soft law’ approach that relies on governance codes and voluntary commitments to improve gender diversity on boards. Progress was minimal, and by 2009, women held just 8.4% of board seats across listed companies, one of the lowest rates in Europe.

The turning point came in January 2011, when the Assemblée Nationale passed the Copé-Zimmermann law. The legislation required all listed companies, as well as non-listed companies employing more than 500 people or generating revenue of over €50 million, to achieve at least 20% gender parity on their boards by 2014, rising to 40% by 2017. The enforcement mechanism was meaningful: companies that failed to comply could not compensate any board members, and new board appointments that did not contribute to the gender parity were automatically invalidated.

Outcomes

By 2020, women represented 44.6% of board directors at CAC 40 companies and 45.2% at SBF 120 companies. By 2024, these figures had risen further to 46.7% and 46.4% respectively, making France not only compliant but a global leader, ranking second worldwide in board gender diversity, behind only Iceland.

Unlike Norway, France also saw a positive shift in shareholder attitudes. A study published by EDHEC Business School, examining over 2,700 director elections between 2007 and 2020, found that shareholder support for female directors increased markedly after the law’s introduction. Female candidates received greater support than male candidates in post-quota elections, suggesting that the quota did not merely fill seats, but actively changed perceptions of women’s qualifications and legitimacy as directors.

Research published in the journal Environmental and Social Governance found that companies with more women on their boards showed measurably improved environmental and social performance. Women directors tended to have more E&S experience than their male counterparts and were shown to steer companies toward more responsible governance practices.

The limitations of the Copé-Zimmermann law mirror Norway’s in one critical respect: the gains did not cascade downward. In 2020, women made up only 21% of executive committee members at the largest French listed companies, and only 10% of those held operational positions. France recognised this gap and, in December 2021, passed the Rixain Act, extending quota obligations to executive committees and senior management, with targets of 30% by 2027 and 40% by 2030.

The verdict: France’s experience is the most convincing evidence that hard law outperforms soft law on this issue. The speed and scale of change following a mandatory quota, backed by meaningful financial penalties, is categorically different from what voluntary measures produced. The lesson for policymakers is that the glass ceiling does not shatter on its own, but also that the glass ceiling in the boardroom is not the same as the one in the executive suite

Case Study 3: India, the minimalist mandate

Legislation

India’s approach to legislating for women in boardrooms takes the form of Section 149 of the Companies Act 2013, that mandated all listed companies and large public companies to appoint at least one woman director to their board. The deadline for compliance was set for April 2015. The Securities and Exchange Board of India subsequently extended the requirement to the top 500 listed firms by April 2019 and the top 1,000 by April 2020. Penalties for non-compliance include fines ranging from INR 50,000 to INR 500,000, with daily fines for ongoing violations.

Unlike the Norwegian and French laws, India did not set a%age threshold. The requirement was simply one woman. This reflects the broader challenge of the Indian corporate context, where, prior to the Act, women were almost entirely absent from boardrooms, and family-controlled conglomerates dominate the listed company landscape.

Outcomes

The law produced a sharp, visible increase in women’s board representation immediately following the April 2015 compliance deadline. A decade on, Nifty-500 companies average approximately one in five board members being women. However, 223 of those 500 companies fulfil precisely the minimum mandate with only one woman director, suggesting that many companies have met the letter of the requirement without embracing its spirit.

Researchers at The Wire and other institutions have found more encouraging signals within the data. Studies using employee review platforms found that firms with higher proportions of women on their boards had measurably better workplace culture scores. Importantly, firms were, on average, appointing more women than the bare minimum required, suggesting that the legal mandate sent a signal that companies internalised beyond mere compliance.

The weaknesses of India’s approach are well-documented. A single mandatory appointment does not constitute critical mass. Research suggests that women need to comprise at least 15% of a board, ideally holding three or more seats, before they can meaningfully influence board deliberations and governance outcomes. One woman in a room of fifteen is tokenism with a legal certificate.

The verdict: India’s Companies Act 2013 opened the door but did not widen it. A minimalist mandate in a country with a deeply patriarchal corporate culture produced incremental compliance rather than transformative change. However, there are signs of positive cultural shifts in firms that have gone beyond the minimum and point to the value of stronger, more ambitious legislation.

What Sri Lanka can learn

Across these three case studies, a clear pattern emerges. Mandatory legislation with teeth delivers measurable results. Soft approaches, voluntary commitments, and governance code nudges do not. Norway’s pioneering law and France’s Copé-Zimmermann Act both demonstrate that gender balance at the board level is achievable, and achievable quickly, when the state decides to require it. India’s experience shows that a minimum mandate is better than nothing, but is insufficient on its own to change corporate culture.

The three important caveats: First, boardroom quotas do not automatically produce pipeline change. In both Norway and France, the gains at the board level have not been replicated in the executive suite, in operational leadership, or across mid-management. Quotas are a ceiling intervention, and they need to be complemented by floor interventions, such as mentoring, sponsorship, pay equity, and care infrastructure, to reshape organisations from within. Second, the quality of women appointed under quotas is not diminished, and thus, the meritocracy argument against quotas does not survive empirical scrutiny. The evidence consistently shows that women appointed to boards following quota legislation are as qualified, or more qualified, than their predecessors. Third, the design of the mandate matters enormously. Effective legislation requires ambitious targets, enforceable consequences, and a genuine commitment to closing not just the board gap but the leadership gap at every level.

Sri Lanka’s consistently low rankings on economic gender parity reflect a structural problem that will not resolve itself incrementally. With 40% of the top 30 CSE-listed companies not having a single woman on their Boards, something must change.  The Women Directors Forum advocates for a considered, evidence-based conversation about whether legislative intervention has a role to play in accelerating change in our boardrooms. The evidence from these three countries suggests it does.

(The author is the Vice-Chair of the Women Directors’ Forum, Sri Lanka Institute of Directors & PhD Candidate in Medical Physics, University of Colombo)

Sources

World Economic Forum, Global Gender Gap Report 2025. https://reports.weforum.org/docs/WEF_GGGR_2025.pdf

Bertrand, M., Black, S.E., Jensen, S. & Lleras-Muney, A. (2019). Breaking the Glass Ceiling? The Effect of Board Quotas on Female Labor Market Outcomes in Norway. The Review of Economic Studies.

Garcia-Blandon, J. et al. (2023). Direct and spillover effects of board gender quotas: Revisiting the Norwegian experience. Business Ethics, the Environment & Responsibility.

EDHEC Business School. (2024). On the Effectiveness of Gender Quotas: Insights from Shareholder Preferences. https://www.edhec.edu

ISS Governance. (2022). https://insights.issgovernance.com

Gide. (2025). Increasing Gender Diversity in the Management Bodies of Major Companies. https://www.gide.com

India Briefing. (2023). Understanding the Mandate for Women Directors Under India’s Company Law. https://www.india-briefing.com

The Wire. (2024). Has the ‘Woman Director’ Mandate Served Corporate India Well? https://m.thewire.in

Chicago Booth Review. Do Quotas for Corporate Boards Help Women Advance? https://www.chicagobooth.edu

Philanthropy Roundtable. (2022). Improving Board Diversity: Lessons from Sweden and Norway. https://www.philanthropyroundtable.org

title: Anuradhapura shift: Beginning ends, end begins | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 17 September 2026 00:00
-     - 12

Have ‘primaries’ for 2029 begun?

Successful event generates high spirits, 

camaraderie

The SLPP’s Anuradhapura rally is occasion for my conclusion that the arc of the AKD Presidency and JVP-NPP rule has begun its parabolic descent. This does not mean a linear trajectory from Anuradhapura 2026 to the President’s House 2029 for Namal Rajapaksa—a scenario which is possible, but far from preordained

My caption this week is an obvious echo of Winston Churchill’s characterisation at a nodal point in WWII, that it was not yet ‘the beginning of the end’, but only ‘the end of the beginning’. Later in the war, he announced the beginning of the end. 

There is usually an interregnum between the two, but sometimes the transition is short, and at others, the end of the beginning marks the beginning of the end.  

‘Why Prabhakaran Will Lose’ was the title of an article by me (then in my late-40s) which appeared prominently in the pages of The Sunday Island, Colombo, dated October 17th 2004. At a time when the political, academic and civic intelligentsia was wedded to the thesis of an ‘unwinnable war’, the title risked damage to my intellectual reputation and credibility by going beyond an assertion of ‘Why Prabhakaran Won’t Win’—which would mean a hurting stalemate—to a definitive ‘will lose’. My unambiguous prediction was made the year before Mahinda Rajapaksa secured his party’s Presidential candidacy, won the Presidency, and appointed Gotabaya Rajapaksa and Sarath Fonseka as Secretary/Defence and Army chief respectively. None of these were safely predictable.   

Though occasioned by Karuna’s rebellion and the intra-LTTE mini civil war in the East, with Karuna already on the backfoot, my prognosis was grounded far more in the comparative study of successful asymmetric wars; Prabhakaran’s sustained transgression of their characteristic features and norms; and the axiom of Vietnam’s General Giap that “if you override the objective laws of development of a phenomenon, those objective laws will override you”. 

Similarly, the SLPP’s Anuradhapura rally is occasion for my conclusion that the arc of the AKD Presidency and JVP-NPP rule has begun its parabolic descent. This does not mean a linear trajectory from Anuradhapura 2026 to the President’s House 2029 for Namal Rajapaksa—a scenario which is possible, but far from preordained.   

Real-time social media coverage and TV newscasts showed that the Anuradhapura rally of the SLPP and partners, with Mahinda Rajapaksa on stage, was discernibly larger than the ruling party’s public meetings in Polonnaruwa and Anuradhapura (the next day), featuring President Anura Dissanayake. 

Anuradhapura was a more organic mass mobilisation. The SLPP rally was energised by a cocktail of strong emotions—overweening affection and respect for Mahinda Rajapaksa, combative loyalty to the incarcerated Namal Rajapaksa, open declaration of a determination to ensure Namal’s election as President in 2029, renewed collective hope at that prospect, defiant resistance to the ruling JVP-NPP and reawakened bitter memories of JVP barbarism in the locality. (Especially poignant was the recollection of the JVP’s murder in 1987 in the Anuradhapura bazaar, of Nandana Marasinghe, a hero of the JVP’s April 1971 uprising). The mood was more upbeat and applause from the audience was far more spontaneous, animated, enthusiastic and frequent at SLPP/Anuradhapura.

With a rampaging national ‘crisis of affordability’ (to borrow New York Mayor Mamdani’s famous phrase), the AKD-NPP bloc will hardly win a two-front battle in the heartland with the SJB and SLPP. The SJB will savage it on economics and governance; the SLPP will do so on economics and nationalism. Because of its small but raucous old allies, the SLPP may forfeit minority votes that Namal could win back, but that won’t save the JVP-NPP since some of its minority votes will go to Sajith and the SJB

It is not that the Anuradhapura discourse didn’t have a downside. There was an occasional infusion of ultranationalism—though not (yet) open chauvinism or racism—coming more from the SLPP’s old allies rather than the SLPP itself.  It was also a pity—or sadly symbolic—that the scheduled closing speech by the SLPP’s DV Chanaka got ‘timed out’ or was somehow ‘crowded out’.  

AKD’s Polonnaruwa and Anuradhapura speeches had nothing of the appeal his oratory had in 2024. The thrill was gone. All he had was a surly negativism, a truculently articulated commitment to ‘lawfare’ (amounting to a McCarthyite witch-hunt) against the Rajapaksa family. No credible, constructive hope for an improved life was communicated. His appeal has been funnelled-down to reassuring and remotivating the JVP-NPP hardcore. The combative cockiness of AKD and other JVP-NPP leaders, is hollow.  

Moral low ground 

AKD has embarked on a highly polarising two-pronged project. The dynamic of polarisation that cannot possibly work in his favour; it can only undermine him and his Government, shrinking its space. 

The first prong is the witch-hunt which as AKD has indicated may well encompass every member of the Rajapaksa family, “the big boss or boss’ son it doesn’t matter”. The public perception is of a move which is intentionally though indirectly aimed at Mahinda. 

Anura and the JVP-NPP do not seem to understand that the legitimacy enjoyed by Mahinda is long, deep and unassailable because his achievement in winning in three years a 30-year war and restoring peace and territorial unity, is historic. That historic legitimacy sheds a penumbra of sympathy in the mass mind, on his son Namal and spouse Shiranthi. 

Mahinda’s legitimacy in the mass-mind, is that of a living legend, rooted in the Mahavamsa matrix of real and mythicised history. Targeting Mahinda’s emotional and physical wellbeing by targeting his family, depletes governmental legitimacy and popularity. 

AKD is indirectly targeting a man and directly targeting the family of that man whose popularity and legitimacy he will never begin to approximate. It is a battle he may win in the post-22A courts but can never win in the hearts and minds of the people. 

The mechanism of jailing people before they are convicted of a crime also raises questions of natural justice. This is more so when it comes to a family that shared deadly risks when its patriarch was leading the country in a titanic war against the world’s worst terrorism. The family could have chosen to spend the war safely overseas in East Asia/Eurasia, but didn’t. 

The Rajapaksa family was punished for its cavalier conduct and unmindful excesses in Government by the electorate which voted them out twice – and overthrew one of them with the most angularities. 

They now seem to be ‘soft targets’ which the JVP was notorious for, e.g., Vijaya Kumaratunga. Public memory will recall the barbaric lethal targeting of relatives and whole families by the JVP in the late 1980s. This time the vengeful targeting of families isn’t lethal but legal.

Mahinda’s legitimacy in the mass-mind, is that of a living legend, rooted in the Mahavamsa matrix of real and mythicised history. Targeting Mahinda’s emotional and physical wellbeing by targeting his family, depletes governmental legitimacy and popularity

The second prong of Anura’s lawfare is the ‘Inquisition’ against the top-brass of the war-winning military; a military perceived as having played the role of liberators of the island’s vast majority. 

Thus, Anura’s double-barrelled campaign is against two targets—the family of Mahinda Rajapaksa, the living national patriarch, and the victorious military high command. These two targets are components of the war-winning ‘power-bloc’, and taken together constitute a single composite target. Such a sweeping witch-hunt of the political and military victors in a historic national war would be riskily destabilising in any post-war society. 

Moreover, AKD’s polarising ‘lawfare’ takes place while the ground the Government stands on is being eroded by the heart-rending economic suffering of “the working poor” as journalist Methmalie Dissanayake has put it in an exceptional piece of social reportage. 

Tri-polar game

The deeper reason which makes Anuradhapura 2026 the end of the beginning and the beginning of the end of AKD-JVP-NPP rule, is systemic. The game has just changed. A bipolar game—JVP-NPP vs. SJB, Anura vs. Sajith—just became tripolar. Namal’s Presidential campaign has been pretty much launched, and the SLPP has revived as a fighting party willing to take the battle to the Government. Even if he remains jailed, ‘Release Namal!’ will be a mobilising slogan in the 2029 campaign in the heartland.

The post-Anuradhapura tri-polarity will damage the Government for two major reasons: 

As foreign experts have pointed out, the debt repayment really starts biting in 2028 and will probably be compounded by the requirements of an unavoidable IMF program when the current one ends in 2027.      

AKD-JVP-NPP will be besieged on two fronts, the centrist/centre-right, and nationalist-populist/statist-populist. The SJB and SLPP will each take a ‘limb’ in its jaws and pull the NPP’s 2024 socio-electoral bloc apart. (The NPP just lost the Eppawela Multi-Purpose Cooperative Society election to the SJB-led Opposition).

With a rampaging national ‘crisis of affordability’ (to borrow New York Mayor Mamdani’s famous phrase), the AKD-NPP bloc will hardly win a two-front battle in the heartland with the SJB and SLPP. The SJB will savage it on economics and governance; the SLPP will do so on economics and nationalism. Because of its small but raucous old allies, the SLPP may forfeit minority votes that Namal could win back, but that won’t save the JVP-NPP since some of its minority votes will go to Sajith and the SJB.

Patriarch returns

If unfairly imprisoned, could ‘Release Namal!’ motivate voters in 2029?

Strictly theoretically, 2029 should be something of a slam-dunk for Sajith, because the unprecedented growth of poverty and inequality should provide a socioeconomic majority for him if he deploys the franchise he holds exclusively, i.e., that of the developmentalist-populist paradigm of his father President Premadasa. Today’s political narrative is also about ‘Fathers and Sons’

The same methodology that prompted me to assert ‘Why Prabhakaran Will Lose’ back in October 2004, helps me envisage the end of the incumbent administration. The great Asian leader and philosopher Mao Zedong’s 50th death anniversary fell this month. When the mighty, industrialised Japanese army invaded China, Mao applied his dialectical mastery of contradictions to military science and wrote the famous text ‘Problems of Strategy in the Anti-Japanese War’, predicting that the Chinese Communist and nationalist forces on the defensive, would, with the passage of time, prevail over the preponderant Japanese forces on the offensive. He explained how the contradictions in the Japanese project would unfold, grow, weakening that dominant invasive force, while the underdog resistance would grow due to objective conditions. 

So also, with the AKD-JVP-NPP rulers and the Opposition. What is currently primary will become secondary, and what is currently secondary will become primary. 

Mao Zedong and General Giap, geniuses of asymmetric conflict, perceived three stages of development: (a) strategic defensive (b) contention or equilibrium (c) strategic counteroffensive. With the SLPP’s fierce fightback in Anuradhapura, the overall political struggle shifted from the Opposition on the strategic defensive and the Govt on the strategic offensive, to the second stage: the Opposition in a mode of contention, and a resultant equilibrium between Government and Opposition in public perception and opinion.   

Sajith and SJB 

It is illogical to accurately condemn the 22nd Amendment as an attempt by the executive to coopt the judiciary, while simultaneously staying non-committal on NR, on the presumption that a transparently fair trial is structurally possible post-22A, especially for a Rajapaksa rival of the rulers. 

Silence is also unwise because AKD will inevitably attempt to entrench his incumbency by using ‘lawfare’ against Sajith and other non-SLPP Opposition candidates too.  

That said, the SLPP’s revival is certain to spur the SJB from trot to canter. 

Strictly theoretically, 2029 should be something of a slam-dunk for Sajith, because the unprecedented growth of poverty and inequality should provide a socioeconomic majority for him if he deploys the franchise he holds exclusively, i.e., that of the developmentalist-populist paradigm of his father President Premadasa. Today’s political narrative is also about ‘Fathers and Sons’.

The game has just changed. A bipolar game—JVP-NPP vs. SJB, Anura vs. Sajith—just became tripolar. Namal’s Presidential campaign has been pretty much launched, and the SLPP has revived as a fighting party willing to take the battle to the Government. Even if he remains jailed, ‘Release Namal!’ will be a mobilising slogan in the 2029 campaign in the heartland

But that’s only theoretically. The reality is that Sajith Premadasa is a social democratic centrist who leads a party which is not. The SJB is a centre-right party with a rightist caucus. Having been under Ranil Wickremesinghe’s leadership, it has no experience of a party and politics chosen by popular vote to lead the country. It therefore lacks the political instincts and reflexes to fight and win. It rejects attempts to change or induct new elements, and inhabits its centre-right cocoon with the only idea buzzing around being an SJB-UNP bloc with a ‘rightist’ ideological identity.  An SJB-UNP bloc isn’t intrinsically bad, but is colossally inadequate—as surgically argued by Kusum Wijetilleke, SJB Working Committee member and Advisor on Political Economy to Sajith Premadasa. Wijetilleke has written what I consider the best think-piece I have read in the local press this year so far. (https://www.ft.lk/columns/Centre-right-Wrong-about-everything/4-797138)

Any SJB-UNP convergence can decisively attract votes only if such a convergence takes place on the basis of a shift to progressive centrism/social democracy and the revival of President Premadasa’s pro-people development paradigm. 

If not, the sheer fatigue of protracted (decades-long) defeat will have the effect on the SJB and UNP that interminable attrition eventually has on all living things: atrophy.     Sticking in its stagnant zone of defunct neoliberal, market-fundamentalist economics makes it problematic for the SJB or an SJB-UNP bloc to defeat the AKD-JVP-NPP bloc. Why so? Because AKD is driving Ranil Wickremesinghe-Mangala Samaraweera-Malik Samarawickrema economics and foreign policy to the next level. The SJB has no problem with that; only with mismanagement and the pace of privatisation (Sri Lankan airlines). 

You cannot fight a battle effectively if you share the same ideological-paradigmatic space as the enemy. Sajith Premadasa certainly doesn’t share AKD’s views on the economy, but the SJB’s lead economist Dr. Harsha de Silva plays softball.  

In the remake of The Magnificent Seven with Denzel Washington (I preferred the 1960 original with Yul Brynner), Ethan Hawke, playing a burnt-out ace marksman and former officer in the defeated Confederate Army, tries to train the hopelessly inaccurate townsfolk in rifle shooting. In frustrated irritation, he yells at one point “you’ve got to hate what you’re shooting at!” – and demonstrates by unerringly shooting the straw heads off the line of scarecrows erected for target practice.  So long as it stays a centre-right party espousing and thereby tacitly endorsing a neoliberal right-wing economic agenda, the SJB can’t ‘hate’ what the AKD-JVP-NPP is doing in economics.  By contrast, the SLPP as a party with a rather more ‘Statist’ Rajapaksa ideology, takes a greater distance from the ruling bloc, and therefore can naturally, instinctively, hit the electoral adversary harder.  

The SJB is the largest single Opposition force on the ground. Riffing on Mao again, while the MR-NR headed SLPP has just become the ‘leading force’ in the Opposition outside Parliament, the SJB remains the ‘main force’ of the Opposition in general.  Therefore, the failure of the SJB to shift to progressive centrism (e.g., the US Democrats) would be a major political tragedy. The SJB is the closest we come to a moderate, pluralist-centrist formation. Sajith is the closest we come to a social democratic inclination, with the ability to deliver an actual poverty-reduction program. Dysfunctionality of the politico-ideological centre in any society, removes an obstacle to the growth of extremes, and accelerates polarisation (often with an ethnoreligious note) in a context of debt-driven economic crisis, povertisation/pauperisation and ‘multidimensional vulnerability’.  

2024 moment is over 

The JVP-NPP won in 2024 because the two main democratic parties were in severe crisis: 

The SLPP lost, crashed and splintered because it had shifted from Mahinda Rajapaksa’s pragmatic-progressivism to Gotabaya’s Far Right ideology, banned imports of agrochemicals overnight, was overthrown by the people, and fissured by clinging to President Ranil Wickremesinghe (the ‘Gas Cylinder’) while Namal Rajapaksa fought bravely to return the party to its roots. 

The SJB which had initiated the Galle Face struggle with a militant march to the Presidential Secretariat and a speech by Sajith challenging Gotabaya, failed to serve as a Premadasa-ist populist Opposition when Ranil’s harsh austerity policy was massively alienating people. SJB’s Harsha and Eran urged—and cheered—“painful” reforms. Sajith failed to veto them and override their line. 

AKD and the JVP-NPP moved into the breach opened by the SLPP and SJB. 

Anuradhapura September 2026 marks the beginning of the end of AKD-JVP-NPP rule because the very basis of the 2024 victory of that bloc has been upended; the very condition that provided for the victory has been abolished. 

With Namal’s imprisonment, Mahinda’s symbolic reappearance and the Anuradhapura fightback, the SLPP is rejuvenated. The SJB is reactivated. The two democratic pillars have re-emerged. The JVP-NPP’s space has structurally shrunk. The 2024 ‘moment’ is over.

title: More than the numbers — how Sri Lanka’s finance professionals can become trusted strategic advisers | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 17 September 2026 00:00
-     - 11

As Sri Lanka continues its economic recovery and reform journey, businesses and policymakers need more than an accurate account of the past. They need finance professionals who can anticipate change, assess risk, identify opportunities and connect financial insight to long-term strategy

Over the past few decades, the profession has evolved beyond a pure compliance remit as we, finance and accounting professionals, have established ourselves as effective business partners. While we still ensure that our organisations meet their legal obligations, we also help to drive business growth, enhance operational efficiency, fund innovation, manage risk and inform leadership decision-making. Undoubtedly, accounting and finance professionals have played a pivotal role in our organisations’ success to date.

Although we have achieved much, we should not be complacent, however. The fast-moving nature of today’s business environment demands that we keep evolving and reinventing ourselves. In fact, I believe we are on the cusp of an exciting inflection point. We are about to make the leap from business partner to strategic adviser, enabled by new technological tools and our enhanced human capabilities. 

As strategic advisers, we will create new value by providing the indispensable insights and knowledge that will enable our organisations to seize new market opportunities, pre-solve major problems and flourish in a world that will be defined by the transition to a more sustainable economy and advances in artificial intelligence (AI). So how can we evolve from where we are now to being the trusted strategic advisers of the future? 

See ourselves as advisers, not technicians. In an era when compliance will increasingly be automated, real-time and embedded into business processes, we should not see our primary function as ticking boxes. Instead, we will be expected to think outside the box, with our advisory identity being central to our professional relevance. Amid a deluge of information – and misinformation – organisational leaders and our peers in other functions will seek us out for our insights, knowledge and ethical judgement. What’s more, as AI transforms what our organisations do and how they do it, we will provide the vital assurance that data and systems are being used competently and responsibly.

Be able to tell the human stories behind the data. Finance and accounting have long been pigeon-holed as a ‘number-crunching’ profession. Sure, we are highly skilled at gathering, managing and presenting data. But it is how we interpret data that will matter in the age of AI. We must be able to understand not only what the data means for our own business, but what it means for our industry, our community and society at large. What are the risks it reveals? And the opportunities? How can we use it to create value? We must use data to look forwards as well as backwards and make insightful predictions about how markets will evolve. 

Have agency and continuously upskill. Becoming a trusted strategic adviser isn’t something that will happen by magic. We must make it happen by investing in our own development. That means learning and enhancing the skills that will enable us to create value in future – skills such as strategic and critical thinking, collaboration and relationship building, and the interpretation of AI output. It should also go without saying that we will need to be accomplished users of AI tools, with the ability to undertake in-depth scenario planning. 

The shift towards becoming a trusted strategic adviser is one of the key themes identified by Rise2040, a profession-wide research initiative launched by AICPA and CIMA. The initiative brings together 6,000 insights from across the globe to collectively explore, challenge and shape the future of public accounting and finance. 

Participants to the research highlighted that accounting and finance professionals will bring discernment, perspective and stability in an era of widespread uncertainty. We will also ‘connect the dots’ that underpin value creation by integrating finance with strategy, operations and technology.

For Sri Lanka, this evolution could hardly be more timely. As the country continues its economic recovery and reform journey, businesses and policymakers need more than an accurate account of the past. They need finance professionals who can anticipate change, assess risk, identify opportunities and connect financial insight to long-term strategy. Sri Lanka has a deep and growing pool of finance and accounting talent. The opportunity now is to harness that talent not only to support recovery, but to help shape the country’s next chapter of sustainable growth.

By embracing the continued evolution of our profession, we can move from being the business partners of today to becoming the trusted strategic advisers of tomorrow, helping lead our organisations successfully into the future.

(The author is Country Head of Sri Lanka, AICPA and CIMA)

title: Technocity | Lenovo Premier League 2026 brings Sri Lanka’s IT community together | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 17 September 2026 00:00
-     - 4

Sri Lanka’s technology industry traded keyboards for cricket bats as the Technocity | Lenovo Premier League 2026 (TLPL 2026) brought together 18 leading companies from the country’s IT  sector for a memorable day of competitive cricket and camaraderie.

More than a corporate cricket tournament, TLPL 2026 was created as a platform to bring together people from across Sri Lanka’s technology ecosystem -not only business owners and managers but employees representing their different organisations.

The event was graced by Technocity Group Chairman Famy Ismail; Laptop.lk Director Minhaj Farook; and Lenovo Sri Lanka Country Business Head Siraj Jabir. 

Commenting on the initiative, Famy Ismail said:”TLPL gives us the opportunity to bring the technology community together in a completely different environment. Business is built on relationships, and events like this allow people to compete passionately while developing friendships that can continue well beyond the cricket field.”

A substantial cash prize of Rs 400,000 was awarded to the Champions, while  Runners-up received Rs 200,000. Cash awards and recognition were also presented for outstanding individual performances, including Best Batsman, Best Bowler and Man of the Match.

However, the recognition did not end with the winning teams.In a special ‘first of its kind’ initiative announced at TLPL 2026, Technocity will take the players from all 18 participating teams, together with their respective team managers, on a fully sponsored one-day adventure and team building experience to Kitulgala, including white water rafting. This  is particularly significant, because many IT industry incentive programmes, overseas tours and partnership events tend to recognise top-performing sales personnel, managers, business owners or selected partners. However TLPL  recognised participating employees of these organisations.

Minhaj Farook said: “Cricket is a great reflection of business. You may have talented individuals, but success comes when everyone understands their role and work towards one goal. TLPL is about bringing that same spirit.”

From the opening huddles and competitive matches to the awards ceremony, Technocity | Lenovo Premier League 2026 delivered an atmosphere of sportsmanship and unity.

With 18 companies competing for exceptional cash prizes and the fact that  every participating team will be  included in the upcoming ‘Kitulgala experience’. Technocity | Lenovo Premier League 2026 demonstrated that the tournament was ultimately about something greater than winning a trophy, it was about bringing an industry together.

title: Lionel Messi set for Argentina farewell in October 6 friendly against Benin | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 17 September 2026 00:00
-     - 4

Messi will make his 208th and final appearance in the ‘farewell he truly deserves’, says Argentina football’s chief.

Lionel Messi was named in Argentina’s squad for a friendly against Benin on October 6, a match that will serve as his farewell appearance after announcing his international retirement last month.

The 39-year-old said in August he was retiring from Argentina duty after a two-decade international career that included winning the 2022 World Cup and Copa America triumphs in 2021 and 2024.

“We made the decision to invite the best player in the world, the symbol of our national team, our captain, Lionel Andres Messi, so that he can have the farewell he truly deserves on October 6 here in Argentina,” said the country’s FA president Claudio Tapia. The match against Benin will take place at River Plate’s Estadio Monumental in Buenos Aires, which can accommodate 85,000 spectators.

Tapia also invited all of Argentina’s 2022 World Cup winners to join Messi for what he said would be an “unforgettable” occasion.

Argentina begin a series of three friendlies against Bolivia on September 30 in Cordoba — their first match since losing the World Cup final to Spain — before taking on Burkina Faso in Buenos Aires on October 3.

Messi has been included in the squad for the third match against Benin, when he is expected to make his 208th and final appearance for the national team. He is Argentina’s all-time record scorer with 125 goals.

Following the death of his father Jorge last month, Messi had said he had “serious doubts” about continuing to play football of any sort for “much longer”.

“It was a decision that hurt and still hurts deep in my soul but I understand that it is the right time,” Messi said when he called time on his Argentina career.

His contract with Major League Soccer club Inter Miami runs until the end of the 2028 season.

title: Eastern Province to host over 1,000 players at EPBA All Island Open Badminton Championships | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 17 September 2026 00:00
-     - 3

The Eastern Province is set to make badminton history by hosting more than 1,000 national ranking players at the EPBA All Island Open Badminton Championships 2026, which will be held from September 22 to 28 at the Mc Heyzer Indoor Stadium in Trincomalee.

Sanctioned by Sri Lanka Badminton (SLB) as a Level 1 National Ranking Tournament, the seven-day championship has attracted an impressive 1,018 entries, bringing together some of Sri Lanka’s leading badminton players across the Junior, Open and Veteran categories.

The tournament carries a total cash prize pool of Rs. 750,000, adding further significance to what is expected to be one of the biggest badminton events ever staged in the Eastern Province.

The large participation is also expected to create a significant economic impact on Trincomalee, with hundreds of players accompanied by families, coaches and supporters. Hotels, restaurants, retail outlets and transport service providers in the area are expected to benefit from the increased influx of visitors during the championship.

The landmark tournament is organised by the Eastern Province Badminton Association (EPBA) under the leadership of Tournament Director Aliyar Faizer and Deputy Tournament Director S. Stanly Prashanth.

The event has also received important grassroots support from Trincomalee’s Spartan Badminton Academy, contributing to the development and promotion of badminton in the Eastern Province.

The EPBA All Island Open Badminton Championships 2026 is expected to provide a valuable platform for Sri Lanka’s emerging junior players, established national-ranked competitors and veteran athletes to compete at a high level while further strengthening the sporting profile of Trincomalee and the Eastern Province.

summary:

The Bahrain National Cricket Team on arrival at the Cinnamon Grand: Front row from left: Amish Rana, Prashant Kurup (Vice captain and wicket keeper), Asif Ali (Captain), Adil Ahmed (Manager),Nazomi Azhar [General Manager Cinnamon Grand), Dharshika de Silva (Director Celebrate Lanka) Nishantha Weerasinghe (Coach), Junaid Niazi, Ali Dawood, Ahmer Bin Naser. 

Standing from left: Imran Javed, Monammed Waseem, Abdul Majid, Rizwan Butt, Yaseer Naser, Asif Shaikh, Sohail Ahmed, Shujath Rasool, Isuru Weerasinghe (Physio)

Text and pic by P D DE SILVA

The Bahrain National Cricket Team after a disappointing performance at the Asian Cricket Council Men’s Premier Cup group stage matches played in Malaysia  a few days back arrived in Sri Lanka to prepare for the upcoming 2026 ICC Men’s T20 World Cup Asia Sub - regional qualifier A which is also scheduled to be hosted in Malaysia from 3 to15 October 2026.

The  ‘2026 ICC Men’s T20 World Cup Asia Sub - regional qualifier A’ forms part of the qualification  pathway for the 2028 T20 World Cup. Teams from Thailand, Kuwait, Bhutan, Qatar, Myanmar, Mongolia and Bahrain are scheduled to participate.

During their 20 day stay in the island,   the Bahrain cricketers will avail the facilities including the coaching staff at Sri Lanka Cricket’s High Performance Centre at Khettarama courtesy SLC and play four practice games at the Galle International Stadium.

The Bahrain National Team led by Asif Ali comprise of Prashant Kurup (Vice captain and wicket keeper),  Amish Rana,  Junaid Niazi, Ali Dawood, Ahmer Bin Naser,  Imran Javed, Monammed Waseem, Abdul Majid, Rizwan Butt, Yaseer Naser, Asif Shaikh, Sohail Ahmed and Shujath Rasool.

The team is managed by Adil Ahmed and Nishantha Weerasinghe is the Head Coach while Isuru Weerasinghe is the Physio. The team’s inbound travel arrangements are being handled by Celebrate Lanka.
